_2026-09-01 — **WS-17 Restore Governance (Implementation Pass 2) COMPLETE. Physical restore is now GOVERNED; it is still never EXECUTED by the platform.** Migration **`0074_stale_rachel_grey`** (ledger `0073` → `0074`), recorded as **§33.11** of `docs/ENTERPRISE_HRMS_MASTER_OWNER_REVIEW.md`. Four tables — restore requests, append-only approvals, append-only executions, append-only validations — plus one additive column, `installations.restore_approval_policy`. **No restore table carries an `organizationId`**, verified against the generated migration, because a physical restore of a shared installation rolls back every customer on it and modelling it as organization-owned would be the most dangerous lie the platform could tell. **Nothing runs `pg_restore`, triggers PITR, rolls back a snapshot or opens a shell; there is no provider credential and no callback secret anywhere in the implementation.** **Production maker-checker cannot be switched off**: `requiresMakerChecker` returns true for production **without consulting the policy column at all**, so no misconfiguration can relax it, and environment naming is never used to infer relaxation — non-production defaults to `always_required` and relaxation is an explicit per-installation act. The comparison is on **immutable user id**, never a name, email or membership, because platform authority is user-scoped. **A partial recovery point is blocked by default**: completeness is derived from recorded backup evidence via `deriveBackupRunResult` and never from a caller flag, a PITR or provider point is honestly `unknown`, and proceeding requires an acknowledgement that **names the missing component**, stored immutably and frozen onto the approval — a recorded risk acceptance, not a dismissed banner, and never a bare `allowPartial=true`. **An approver approves a blast radius, not an id**: affected organizations are snapshotted at submission, re-derived at approval and re-derived again before dispatch; if the set changed, dispatch is blocked and the approval is invalidated — the approval row is stamped, never rewritten, and the request returns for renewed approval. Proved by test: linking a fourth organization after approval blocks dispatch. **Execution success is not validation success** — separate states, separate evidence; a restore stops at `succeeded` until validation concludes, an `unknown` check never counts as passed, and **an operator attestation can never override an automated failure**. **Nothing pretends**: an executor that cannot take a pre-restore checkpoint yields `unsupported_acknowledged`, never `satisfied`; the platform never claims it stopped traffic; and after dispatch it never claims it cancelled infrastructure work it does not control. **Typed confirmation is target-bound** — `RESTORE <installationKey> <ENVIRONMENT>`, matched exactly server-side; a generic `RESTORE`, a checkbox, or another installation's phrase is refused. **Dispatch is idempotent by caller-supplied key**, so a double-click or retried HTTP call returns the same execution rather than starting a second physical restore; a retry after failure creates a **second attempt** with both preserved, and a completed attempt can never be rewritten into a different outcome. **Drift is split by severity**: installation, environment, restore point or blast radius changing **invalidates approval**, while a new deployment, commit or migration version leaves approval standing but demands **re-acknowledgement**. **Restore tests may never target production**, enforced server-side rather than hidden in a UI, and they reuse the same workflow through a `purpose` dimension so there is no second state machine to drift. **Observed metrics are facts, not verdicts** — recovery-point age, execution duration, validation completion — kept strictly separate from configured targets with no compliance claim; the payload deliberately exposes no `rpoCompliant`/`rtoCompliant`/`slaMet` field. **Fleet Health gained a restore overlay**: an installation with a restore in flight reads `degraded` rather than inheriting healthy pre-restore telemetry that describes a system which no longer exists, and a failed execution or validation reads `unhealthy`. **The UI exists to make blind approval impossible** — before deciding, an approver sees the installation, whether it is production, the recovery point, whether it covers files as well as the database, which risks were accepted and by whom, exactly which organizations are affected, and any drift since the request; every state renders a word and a reason, never colour alone. **WS-21 — Tenant Recovery & Portability is now registered** (P2; selective logical recovery/export/import of one organization without physically rolling back its neighbours; reuses WS-7 primitives and WS-17 evidence; depends WS-7 + WS-17) and is **NOT implemented** — three distinct concepts with three owners: **WS-17** physical infrastructure recovery, **WS-21** logical tenant recovery, **WS-20** legacy/manual onboarding. **Automated executor callbacks remain deliberately unimplemented**: they need per-installation credential issuance, rotation, revocation and storage — a secrets subsystem this pass does not build — and a shared secret would be exactly the unsafe shortcut the freeze warned against; a trusted platform operator records external evidence through the authenticated surface, and the data model is shaped so a future callback needs no schema change. **39 new tests**, covering authority both ways, production self-approval refusal, relaxed-vs-default non-production policy, partial-point blocking and acknowledged exception, target-bound confirmation, blast-radius drift, checkpoint and quiescence preconditions, approval expiry, dispatch idempotency, retry preserving both attempts, execution-vs-validation separation, attestation refusal, restore-test production rejection, health overlay, and observed metrics carrying no SLA verdict. One test-isolation defect of my own was found and fixed rather than worked around: the revocation scenario had revoked a shared fixture's grants, so it now uses a dedicated user. Backend **2986/2987 across 168 files**; the single failure is the **documented WS-6 unscoped `claimDueJobs` suite-isolation condition**, which passes **1/1 alone on a clean database** and whose paths this diff does not touch — the run is recorded as 2986/2987 and **not restated as a clean sweep**. The delta from Slice 1's 2948 is exactly the 39 new tests. Frontend regression green, all three builds succeed, workspace typecheck clean, codegen verified deterministic across two consecutive runs, **API 756 operations across 613 paths** (was 744/602 — +12 operations, +11 paths, all platform-restore), zero duplicate operation IDs, zero dangling schema references, migration `0074` round-trip up → down → up verified with RLS restored on all four tables, drift clean. **Restore history is strong audit evidence: no ordinary hard-delete route, no destructive retention job, no invented retention duration.** **Explicitly NOT implemented: live restore execution, provider restore integration, automated callback ingestion, callback credential lifecycle, the universal self-hosted agent, logical tenant recovery (WS-21), the Enterprise Migration Centre (WS-20), and production deployment.** No real restore or backup was executed, no provider infrastructure contacted, no Production or WWM contact; the disposable database was torn down afterwards. **WS-17 now covers deployment history, backup control/evidence, Fleet Health and restore governance; remaining operational scope is the subject of a final closure review.**_


_2026-08-31 — **WS-17 (Deployment & Backup Operations) Implementation Slice 1 COMPLETE. Restore explicitly DEFERRED. WS-17 is NOT complete.** Deployment history, backup policy/request/evidence, Fleet Health signals and telemetry, on **migration `0073`** (ledger `0072` → `0073`); recorded as **§33** of `docs/ENTERPRISE_HRMS_MASTER_OWNER_REVIEW.md`. **The binding principle: the HRMS is a control and governance plane; infrastructure executes.** There is no shell, no command execution, no remote-management surface and no provider credential anywhere in the implementation. **"Release-pipeline Levels 3–6" was REMOVED from the WS-17 register row rather than invented**: a repository-wide search of every `.md`, `.ts` and `.yml` file plus git history found exactly two occurrences — the register row itself and a status entry quoting it — and nothing anywhere defines Level 3, 4, 5 or 6, with §15 deferring to "§107–§120" sections that are not in this repository. No maturity model was substituted, because inventing one would give fabricated terminology the authority of a frozen requirement. **WS-20 — Enterprise Migration Centre is now registered** in §20 (P2; Super-Admin-enabled per-organization onboarding from legacy systems, spreadsheets and paper records; staged upload → parse → validate → preview → correct → approve → import → reconcile; provenance and original effective dates; migration batches; source-document linkage; resumable/idempotent imports; temporary Migration Officer authority; future human-verified OCR/AI extraction; depends on WS-7 and WS-5) — **it extends WS-7's migration foundations rather than replacing them, and is NOT implemented**; it is emphatically not the WS-17 storage migration tooling. **Installation authority is strict: not one of the six new tables has an `organizationId` column**, verified against the generated migration. One installation serving three organizations produces **one** deployment, **one** backup run and **one** health state, with affected tenants derived through `installation_organizations` — fabricating three backup rows for one `pg_dump` would tell three customers that three backups happened when one did. **Platform authority required a new axis, and the reason is concrete**: `hasPermission` resolves through `membership_roles` and so needs an organization membership, while `seed-roles-permissions.ts` grants the super-admin role `PERMISSIONS.map((p) => p.key)` — **every** key, blanket — so putting platform keys in that catalogue would have handed every super-admin every dangerous mutation automatically and made platform keys tenant-assignable. `platform_operation_grants` therefore grants on the **user** axis, following the shape `break_glass_grants` already established. **Authority is always a conjunction — platform context AND a live grant of the specific key** — proved both ways by test: a granted tenant user is refused, and an ungranted super-admin is refused. Five keys ship (`platform.fleet.read`, `platform.deployment.manage`, `platform.backup.policy.manage`, `platform.backup.request`, `platform.backup.evidence.record`); **`platform.restore.request` and `platform.restore.approve` are RESERVED — declared, never granted, never checked** — because the frozen maker-checker rule is only expressible if the two are separate keys from the outset. **Only a `succeeded` deployment advances installation current state**; a failed one is retained in full as history but never makes the version it tried to install look live. **Backup target is separated from observation** in two tables so "we configured an RPO" can never read as "we met an RPO"; **RPO/RTO are nullable with no defaults** and no observed RTO is offered at all, since it is not inferable from backup timestamps. **The overall backup result is DERIVED from component results and never accepted from the caller**, so a database-only backup is `partial`, never complete — the storage-durability finding made structural, with `unknown` explicitly not `covered`. **A request is not a backup**: an explicit state machine refuses illegal transitions, and reaching `succeeded` there is still not evidence. **Corrections append and supersede rather than rewriting history.** **Fleet Health derives eight signals and exposes NO composite score** — a weighted number would be arithmetic dressed as insight while most installations report nothing, and "backup evidence overdue" serves an operator better than a percentage hiding which of six things is wrong. **Unknown is first-class and never healthy**; `stale` is distinct from unknown; overdue requires a configured cadence, because without an expectation nothing can be late; and **there is no manual health override anywhere** — an administrator cannot paint a signal green. Signals nothing reports (SSL, CPU, disk, provider) are simply absent rather than fabricated. **Telemetry is current-state only, one row per installation**, deliberately not a snapshot lake that would demand destructive pruning no policy authorizes; out-of-order replays are ignored rather than allowed to overwrite fresher truth. **The universal agent and unauthenticated ingestion are deferred, and the boundary was reported rather than crossed**: agent-facing ingestion needs per-installation credentials with issuance, rotation and revocation — a secrets-management subsystem this slice does not build, and a weaker version would have been exactly the unsafe shortcut the freeze warned against. **Retention is policy-driven with no hard-coded durations and no destructive pruning job.** The UI is a restrained Fleet section on the existing platform-admin page: every state renders a **word and a reason**, never colour alone, and there are **no restore controls**. **28 new tests**, all passing first run, covering authority both ways, grant separability, revocation and expiry, shared-hosting fan-out, deployment current-state asymmetry, no-default RPO/RTO, database-only-is-never-complete, request≠backup, illegal transitions, append-and-supersede corrections, unknown/stale/healthy/unhealthy derivation, telemetry replay safety, single-row telemetry, cadence-conditional overdue, and that no document metadata crosses into operational views. Backend **2948/2948 across 167 files — clean sweep, zero failures**; the delta from Pass 2's 2920 is exactly the 28 new tests. Frontend regression and all three builds green; workspace typecheck clean; codegen deterministic; **API 744 operations across 602 paths** (was 732/594 — +12 operations, +8 paths, all platform-operations), zero duplicate operation IDs, zero dangling schema references; migration `0073` round-trip up → down → up verified with RLS restored on all six tables; drift clean. **NOT implemented and explicitly deferred: restore request, approval, execution and testing; production restore; the universal self-hosted agent; incident management (Fleet Health emits signals a later capability may consume — no `incidents` table was created because a health state went red); feature flags; maintenance records; destructive operational-history retention; and the Enterprise Migration Centre.** No production deployment, no live telemetry configured, no real backup policy created, no backup or restore executed, no Production or WWM contact; the disposable database was torn down afterwards. **WS-17 remains INCOMPLETE — restore governance is its next gated pass.**_

Because `null` cannot be distinguished between *disabled* and *unauthorized*, **counts and badges leak nothing about what exists**, which is what makes an HR Oversight queue safe at all. **HR Oversight creates no new read authority**: every row and every count still requires the source module's own permission, so an actor who cannot see a grievance through Employee Relations sees no grievance row, **no grievance count**, and nothing from which to infer a hidden case — and since §28.17 and §30.17 deliberately withhold the grievance and succession keys from `org_admin`, **`org_admin` gains nothing from WS-15 existing**. There is **no Action Centre backdoor**, and **no `action_centre.*` permission is minted at all** (P1), following the Manager Portal precedent of shipping with zero new permissions; navigation may decide whether to show the entry but can never be authority to read source data. **Ten independent authority resolvers ship today and none is unified** — three different resolver enumerations exist (WS-9 Recruitment, WS-10 Onboarding's five-value resolver, WS-13 Requests), and merging them is **OD #14/#15 work belonging to WS-16**, which WS-15 expressly does not claim. **A documentation defect was found and corrected**: the §20 register has assigned **OD #14 and #15 to WS-16 since the original freeze**, and §22 rows 14/15 both read APPROVED/P2, yet the statement *"OD #14 and OD #15 remain approved and unassigned"* had been carried forward through §28.29, §29 and §30.29–30.30 — inaccurate in one word. Four occurrences are corrected to *approved and assigned to WS-16, which has not started*; **the substantive frozen text of both Owner Decisions is untouched and neither is reopened**. **Inline action is allow-listed to exactly four** — Leave approve/reject, Learning enrolment approve/reject, Onboarding task completion and WS-14 skill verification — each invoking the owning module's existing command, re-checking live authority **at action time**, and preserving the source transaction, idempotency guard, audit, notifications and maker-checker; **no approval logic is copied into WS-15**, and if Pass 2 finds one of the four lacks a safe source command it becomes deep-link-only rather than being reimplemented. Everything sensitive or complex is **deep-link-only**: Recruitment staged approval, Employee Relations decisions, WS-13 data-change and fulfilment, succession, Payroll, Lifecycle, Assets/Inventory and Performance scoring. **Nineteen modules were classified with reasons**, and not every module appears: **Payroll is deferred from P1** because its only actionable state is a run-level administrative step with no employee subject, no due date and no safe generic row that improves on its own gated pages; **Assets, Office Inventory and Attendance are excluded** — the first two operational rather than HR, and Office Inventory's effective-dated delegation is precisely what WS-16 exists to generalize, so pulling it in would risk generalizing OD #15 by accident. **Half the candidate sources have no deadline at all**, so `dueAt` and `overdue` are `null` — never `false`, because "not overdue" and "no concept of overdue" are different statements — **deadlines are never manufactured**, SLA is never derived from age, and **Employment Lifecycle effective dates are expressly not relabelled as task due dates**. **No universal priority model is created** (no two sources share a comparable scale, so P1 exposes none), and **no employee-sensitive case is ranked algorithmically**. Sorting is a deterministic four-tier order — overdue by `dueAt`, then due-soon, then undated oldest-first, then a stable tie-break — which **deliberately departs from Manager Portal's `createdAt DESC`**, recorded as a departure rather than left as an inconsistency. **An ESS My Actions surface is approved but frozen to three allow-listed sources** whose authoritative pending state was each confirmed in the repository — `employee_self` onboarding tasks, `document_acknowledgements` with real `dueAt`, and `awaiting_employee` service requests — with own Leave history, Learning progress, performance history, skill claims awaiting HR, Payroll, grievances, succession and notifications **deliberately excluded** because none is work the employee is being asked to do. **Two additions this section makes explicit**: a provider that fails operationally is surfaced as a **named unavailable state, distinct from disabled and from empty**, because *"a systemic error is never silently hidden in a way that leads a user to believe the queue is complete"*; and rendering a redacted row records **no** sensitive-read audit event, so no read is double-counted, with the owning module's OD #18 audit remaining authoritative at the deep link. The three non-P1 bundles are frozen with their own architectures and priorities: **Manager Portal completion (P2)** closes a precisely-identified Recruitment participation gap — panel membership, an outstanding own scorecard, hiring-manager standing — reusing the already-shipped `resolveInterviewVisibilityContext`/`resolveScorecardVisibilityContext` rather than building a second manager authority system; **Employee 360 (P2/P3)** is frozen as bounded module-aware read providers with **no giant employee DTO**, after discovery found the employee detail page shows the **legacy** free-text skills and legacy disciplinary records while WS-11 terms, WS-12 cases, WS-13 requests, WS-14 skills, Leave, Learning, Attendance and Onboarding are absent entirely — so it is not merely incomplete but in two places out of date, and the legacy-versus-successor question is frozen as a presentation reconciliation that **must never become a data migration**; and **Reporting consolidation (P3)** records that **47 report definitions are seeded with permission keys but only 3 generic runners exist**, the other 44 returning 404 from the generic endpoint while reachable through eight bespoke module routes — a valid consolidation target where each report stays permission-scoped and source-owned, with **no single giant report query**, and which is **expressly not an Action Centre defect**. **Cross-module export and sensitive full-text search are not authorized in P1**, being the two features most able to undo redaction. **No AI** may prioritize, approve, infer severity, rank employees or determine succession urgency. **§31.34 freezes a fourteen-row frontend acceptance table** naming actor, surface, provider, read capability, required write action, inline-versus-deep-link and source authority — stated that way for the same reason §29.17 and §30.26 were, so no Pass-2 report may describe a required write as "API-only" — and **§31.35 freezes a 22-invariant Pass-2 test matrix** including the Action Centre backdoor test, maker-checker survival, double-click idempotency on all four inline actions, and the changed-reporting-manager authority-loss case, with a dedicated live suite planned because tenant isolation and permission filtering are database behaviour. Five items are deliberately left conditional on repository evidence at implementation time. No code, schema, migration, permission, API, frontend or WWM change accompanied this pass — the diff is documentation-only. _2026-08-29 — **WS-13 (Employee Data Change Approval & HR Service Requests) complete.** Thirteenth implementation workstream, built to the architecture frozen as §29 — see `docs/EMPLOYEE_REQUESTS.md`. **Eight new tables, migration `0069`, purely additive (zero drops, zero altered columns), RLS with zero policies on all eight, up/down/up verified on a fresh database with `employees` confirmed unchanged at 36 columns throughout, zero schema drift.** **The repository fact that shaped the whole workstream**: an employee could not change their own record at all — `PATCH /employees/:id` is gated on `employee.write` and the only self-service writes were profile-picture upload and delete — so a data-change request is **not a gate over an existing path, it IS the path**, which is why the ESS surface is first-class rather than a convenience. **WS-8's pre-recorded contract was fulfilled exactly**: §24.23 named Employee Data Change as a future consumer of form submissions, and `custom_form_submissions` stays a bare record with **no status and no lifecycle** — WS-13 adds the lifecycle above it and adds no workflow columns to WS-8's tables. **One architecture, two origins**: origin is decided by the ROUTE, never the body; the ESS body carries **no employee identifier at all**, so tampering cannot make a request somebody else's, and both a frontend test and a live test prove it. **The eligible-field registry is an explicit allow-list of 16 personal fields**, with `employmentStatus`, separation, position, department, branch, reporting manager, hire and probation dates, employment type, employee number, notes, Payroll banking/statutory, Leave, Assets, Office Inventory, disciplinary/grievance state and Identity & Access **excluded by construction** — a live test asserts each is refused and the employee row is untouched, because `employees` mixes three ownership classes in one row and a registry keyed on "this column exists" would be a route into separation, promotion and banking. **Configuration can never introduce a field**: `setFieldPolicy` validates against the registry before storing, and a stale row naming an unregistered key is inert. **Four rules hold, each proven live.** (1) **Maker-checker** checks BOTH user id and membership id, and the obvious evasion is impossible because `organization_memberships` is unique on (user, organization) — the loophole is closed by the schema, not by a check somebody could forget. (2) **Stale protection is PER FIELD**, re-checked at decision time *and again* at application time, marking the request `stale` for audited re-confirmation rather than silently overwriting — and **an edit to an unrelated column does not invalidate an untouched request**, which is why `employees.updatedAt` is only a coarse signal. (3) **One active request per (employee, field)** as a partial unique index over active statuses only, so rejected history is fully preserved. (4) **No scheduled application**: `effectiveDate` is a business fact, there is deliberately no "apply due changes" handler, and `applyRequest` is unreachable from any job (§29.11). **Application is transactional and idempotent** — the status guard is re-asserted INSIDE the transaction so two concurrent applies cannot both pass, a retry returns the same `appliedAt` with exactly one `applied` event, and a failure is recorded as `application_failed` with its reason rather than pretending success. Four instants stay distinct: requested, decided, effective, applied. **WS-13 builds its own namespaced stages and resolvers** modelled on WS-9 with a **stage count frozen at request time**; **shipped Recruitment is untouched and not made to depend on WS-13**, and **OD #14 and #15 are expressly not claimed** — no cross-product approval engine, no delegation framework, and assignment for fulfilment is explicitly routing rather than delegation. **OD #23 masking is reused, never reimplemented**: `nationalId` and `passportNumber` are masked in the approval DTO, chronology, audit and reports while the authoritative column keeps the real value — masking governs who may see it, not what is stored, and a live test asserts the secret appears in `employees` and in none of the four surfaces. **Being an approver expands no visibility**: `toApprovalView` is built field by field and never spreads the employee record. **HR Service Requests ship as a configurable catalogue, not a process designer**, with **approval and fulfilment as separate states** so "approved but not yet done" is representable; **WS-13 generates no documents** — a letter request is fulfilled by attaching a WS-5 `generated_documents` record, a document-fulfilled type cannot be fulfilled without one, and a cross-tenant document is refused. **A request for a letter and automatic lifecycle-event letter generation remain separate concepts, so WS-11.1 stays deferred.** **ESS visibility defaults to private at the database** (`visibleToEmployee` false), filtered in SQL and again in the view, with somebody else's request returning **404 rather than 403**. **Eight permission keys**; self-service mints none, Organization Admin holds all eight while maker-checker still stops them approving their own request, and `hr_manager` is withheld both `configure` keys. **Four WS-6 job types, all observers** — none may approve, reject, apply or fulfil, and a test asserts no registered job type anywhere matches that shape. **The §29.17 operational-UI table is satisfied**: three surfaces ship — an ESS `My Requests` page with both submission forms, an HR `Requests & Approvals` workspace with propose/approve/reject/return/re-confirm/apply and acknowledge/approve/reject/fulfil, and a `Request Settings` configuration page — and **this is explicitly NOT the org-wide HR Action Centre**, which remains WS-15's; a test asserts the workspace aggregates no other module. **26 new live tests, all executed** (they caught a real defect: the duplicate-pending unique violation went unrecognized because drizzle wraps the driver error and the SQLSTATE sits on `cause` — fixed by walking the cause chain). **17 new frontend tests** covering the frozen write paths and the unauthorized case. Backend **2713/2713 across 155 files with every live suite enabled and zero skipped**, frontend **790/790 across 71 files**, workspace typecheck clean, all builds succeed, codegen deterministic, no duplicate operation IDs among 691 operations, zero schema drift, ledger **0069**. **One honest caveat**: this machine's default vitest fork pool intermittently fails to start workers and silently drops frontend test files; the complete green result above is from the threads pool, and running the suite in two halves on the fork pool is likewise 70/70 files green — the same contention pattern recorded in WS-10, WS-11 and WS-12. No WWM configuration, no production change. **WS-11.1 remains deferred. OD #14 and #15 remain approved and unassigned. WS-14 has NOT been started — awaiting Owner authorization.**_

Authority is re-resolved at each decision; every decision snapshots stage, resolver, **authority basis** and actor name, so replacing a head or reconfiguring the chain never rewrites history (proven by test). **Offer accept/decline/withdraw** are now reachable and bound to an exact version; **expiry is computed from the authoritative date, not scheduled** (a job could only lag the truth — WS-6 is used for reminders only). **Candidate response links** reuse the platform's existing candidate-token precedent but are deliberately hardened beyond it — SHA-256 hashed rather than plaintext, single-use, version-bound, revocable, uniform 404 on every failure mode — with **no candidate accounts and no e-signature platform** invented. **Employment particulars** (Act 651 §13 / Schedule 1) as a separate versioned record rather than sixteen columns on `offer_versions`, chosen so later lifecycle workstreams can reuse it without an offer; **frozen at issuance** so a statement already furnished never changes when policy is later edited (proven by renaming the organization post-issuance). **No probation duration, notice period or leave entitlement is computed or hard-coded** — unknowable fields are suggested blank rather than guessed. Document generation is **WS-5's only**, wiring the reserved `letterTemplateId`/`generatedDocumentStorageKey` columns and adding 17 `particulars.*` merge fields to WS-5's allow-list. **Conversion is not rebuilt** — only its eligibility guard, scoped to the Recruitment path and **conditional by adoption** (authorization required only where stages are configured; acceptance only where an offer exists), so direct creation, legacy import, WS-7 migration and rehire are unaffected and no historical conversion is invalidated. **No new permission key was minted**; a security fact shaped the gates — the seeded `employee` role holds `offer.manage`, so consequential actions are gated on `offer.issue`/`offer.withdraw`/`candidate.manage`/`recruitment_settings.manage` instead. **Three real defects found and fixed**: a source-validation query that post-checked one arbitrary row's owner and so denied legitimate org-defined codes; the conversion route returning 500 rather than 409 for the new lifecycle errors; and — discovered while wiring WS-9 — **WS-8's `/custom-fields` and `/custom-forms` routes were never actually added to App.tsx**, so those nav links hit NotFound; my earlier patch's route insertion had silently failed and I verified only the import. All three fixed. **Known limitations, stated not implied**: no CAPTCHA provider (interface deferred per §25.14 rather than committing to a vendor), **no malware scanning anywhere in the platform**, no approval delegation (pending WS-16's generalized primitive), and requisition approval still uses its existing single-step service. _2026-08-27 — **WS-8 (Custom Fields & Form Builder) complete.** Eighth implementation workstream, built to the scope frozen as §24 of the Master Owner Review — see `docs/CUSTOM_FIELDS_AND_FORMS.md`. Organizations can now add their own structured data to approved record types and compose it into forms **without a customer-specific source-code fork**, which is the mechanism the platform's "one shared foundation" principle depends on. **Six tables, migration `0064`, additive, RLS-enabled with zero policies on all six, up/down/up verified live.** The split that shapes the whole design: definitions are organization **configuration** (portable by stable `fieldKey`/`formKey`), values and submissions are tenant-isolated **business data** — and business values never live inside configuration JSON. **No dynamic DDL anywhere**: a custom field never becomes a physical column and no domain table is ever `ALTER`ed. **Scope binding is an enum, not a table name** — the six approved scopes are the allow-list, so the prohibited domains (payroll transactions/runs, leave, attendance, asset and inventory movements, disciplinary findings, audit records, security identities) are unreachable by construction rather than by a remembered rule; every read/write additionally re-verifies the target record belongs to the caller's organization. **Both optional reference types were implemented** (`employee_reference`, `master_data_reference`) after confirming the repository already had cheap org-scoped lookups for each; both validate same-organization ownership. No formulas, JavaScript, SQL, scripts, HTML or file-upload fields — there is no expression evaluator in this feature at all, so organization-supplied content has no execution path. **Versioning is real**: stable field identity, one `isCurrent` version enforced by a partial unique index, and every stored value records the `definitionVersionId` it was captured under, so an old value is never reinterpreted through today's configuration; breaking changes (type change, removing an in-use choice, changing a master-data domain) are **refused with 409** once values exist rather than reinterpreting data. Required is **prospective only** — existing records report `missingRequired` and no value is ever fabricated. **Conditional visibility is evaluated server-side on the write path**, so a hidden field cannot be set by crafting a request (422), and it is evaluated against the post-write state so a field made applicable by another value in the same request is accepted. Sensitive fields mask by default, reveal only under a separately-granted `custom_fields.sensitive.read` (registered but granted to **no role**, per the payroll precedent), and reveals are audited; sensitive values never enter logs or audit metadata, and are **omitted entirely** from CSV export unless authorized rather than masked-but-present. **No per-field ACLs**: configuration uses the four `custom_fields`/`custom_forms` keys, while values follow the target domain's own permission — so this is not a second authorization model over employee data. Forms are an ordered-section editor (no drag-and-drop, HTML, CSS or scripting), publish-freezes a version, and a submission snapshots the field label, type and version so historical submissions render exactly as submitted after later edits; submissions reject extra fields (no mass assignment) and reject a superseded `formVersionId`. ESS resolves the target employee **server-side** from the caller's own identity — a supplied `entityId` is ignored rather than validated. No repeating/nested groups, no generic approval engine, no anonymous/public forms, no global-search indexing. Core platform fields are deliberately **not** exposed to the form builder, which removes the "administrator types `employees.bankAccountNumber`" hazard entirely. Integration contracts documented for **WS-10** (`onboarding` is definable but `bindable: false` — one flag and one lookup when WS-10 ships an authoritative record; WS-8 fabricates nothing), **WS-9** (candidate scopes and form type exist; public flow stays with WS-9) and **WS-7** (`setValuesForEntity` is the stable import contract; the adapter was deliberately not wired, since it was not needed to close WS-8 and would have meant touching WS-7's registry for a capability nobody has asked to import). **Two real bugs found and fixed during implementation**: a block comment terminated early by `*/` inside a permission-key example, and — more substantively — the values panel mirrored server state through an effect keyed on query-result identity, an infinite render loop that only surfaced because a test's mock returned a fresh object each render; replaced with a render-time edit overlay that needs no effect. _2026-08-27 — **WS-7 post-completion reconciliation: COMPLETE AFTER TARGETED HARDENING, with one item BLOCKED on an Owner decision.** A review of the four points WS-7's own final report disclosed found that two of them had been reported wrongly, and fixed both. **(1) Payroll opening balances — capability withdrawn, not delivered.** WS-7 claimed "no payroll-opening-balance table exists, so opening balances import as ordinary compensation components." That reasoning was wrong and the implementation was actively unsafe: `createCompensationComponent` always inserts an OPEN (`validTo` null) row, `resolveCompensationAsOf` treats an open row as `validTo = Infinity` so it matches every future pay date, and `calculateEmployeePayroll` adds each resolved component's full amount to `grossEarnings` on every run — an imported one-time balance would have been **paid again every period, forever, taxed and pensioned as ordinary income**. Separately, that function closes any earlier open row for the same `(employee, category, componentTypeCode)`, so mapping a balance onto `basic_salary` would have **silently terminated the employee's real salary row** — a direct breach of the "no silent salary overwrite" constraint. Both confirmed by reading the live, shipped Payroll engine, not inferred. The `payroll_opening_balance` adapter is now **unregistered**, which blocks upload/validation/execution completely (the registry is the allow-list every path checks); the file is retained with the full analysis. The real gap — the platform models no balance/brought-forward/YTD concept anywhere, and `employee_statutory_identifiers` holds SSNIT/TIN identifiers but no contributed-to-date amounts, so a mid-year cutover cannot compute correct graduated PAYE or apply the pension ceiling — is documented with the smallest proposed addition, **awaiting Owner approval; deliberately not built.** **(2) Transaction model — reconciled, not defended.** WS-7 shipped universal per-row commit. Review found the pre-existing legacy importer already commits many employees plus number allocations and personnel files in ONE transaction, proving atomicity achievable for exactly the primitives WS-7's structure/employee adapters reuse. Execution now resolves a policy per batch: **ATOMIC** (single transaction, all-or-nothing, HTTP 422 + `rolledBack: true` on failure) when every entity type in the batch is `transactional` and it is within 2,000 rows; **BATCHED_RESUMABLE** otherwise. The resumable path is retained only where a domain service commits on its own connection (`employment_history`, `qualification`, `certification`, `leave_balance`) — wrapping those would produce a *false* atomicity guarantee, telling the administrator "nothing was written" while rows had committed. The policy is computed automatically (no user option), returned by the API, and **shown in the UI before approval**, naming the specific entity types that prevent rollback. Enabling atomic mixed batches required making `assertBelongsToOrganization`, `assertEmployeeReferencesValid`, `assertValidDepartmentPlacement` and `assertValidPositionPlacement` accept an optional transaction client (additive, defaulted to `db`, every existing call site unchanged) — without it a batch creating a department and its employees together failed its own cross-org check, a real bug caught by the new atomic test. **(3) Legacy importer — end-state defined**, retained unmodified as the compatibility surface with explicit authoritative/deprecation/removal conditions; deliberately NOT routed through the new engine, which would change a working shipped API's observable behaviour for no caller benefit. **(4) `.env` credential — WS-7's report was WRONG and is corrected: it points at the project's own hosted DEVELOPMENT database, not production.** Evidence: repo docs name that project ref as "the development Supabase project" throughout, `NODE_ENV=development`, `APP_BASE_URL=http://localhost:5173`, and no separate production project is documented anywhere. _2026-08-25 — **WS-5 (Documents & Records Foundation) complete.** Fifth implementation workstream from the frozen Master Owner Review — see `docs/DOCUMENTS_AND_RECORDS.md` for the full record. Implements Owner Decision #4 (shared document infrastructure — storage, security, versioning, access control, audit, retention, metadata — while preserving domain-specific ownership tables). **Personnel Files boundary held**: `personnel_files`/`personnel_file_volumes`/`personnel_file_movements`/`records_locations` carry zero storage columns and were verified to have zero column overlap with any digital-document table; all six pre-existing document/personnel-file schemas are untouched by migration `0060`, and `employee_documents`/`candidate_documents` keep their existing routes, permissions, and UI unchanged. Eight new tables: the missing organization-level repository (`organization_documents` + immutable `organization_document_versions`), the shared checklist primitive (`document_requirements`), the shared retention/legal-hold/disposal primitive (`document_retention_records`), the template/generation engine (`document_templates` + `document_template_versions` + `generated_documents`), and per-category behavior (`document_category_settings`) — the category *list* itself reuses the pre-existing organization-defined `document_category` Master Data domain rather than a second management surface. **Version integrity is enforced by the database, not convention**: partial unique indexes guarantee exactly one `current` document version and at most one `active` template version, proven live by hand-forging a second row and by racing two concurrent uploads. Verification is separable from upload (`document.verify`); disposal is separable from management (`document.retention.manage`, deliberately seeded to **no role** — authorizing destruction of records is a per-organization delegation, not implied by HR authority). Archive never deletes, disposal eligibility is a reviewable determination and never automatic, legal hold blocks disposal regardless of elapsed retention, and there is deliberately no bulk-disposal path anywhere. **Output-format decision**: the repository had no PDF tooling at all, so rather than add a rendering dependency on a path that renders organization-controlled input, WS-5 ships a small dependency-free PDF writer — generated letters are plain text, needing no images, vector graphics, or font embedding — which also makes output byte-deterministic (no `/CreationDate`), the property that makes the immutability guarantee checkable rather than merely asserted. Merge fields are an **allow-list, not a sandbox**: content is plain text, substitution is one regex over allow-listed tokens, nothing is ever evaluated, so there is no SSTI surface to sandbox — verified against expression-injection, block-helper, prototype-pollution, and constructor-escape payloads, and the allow-list is asserted to contain no banking/salary/statutory-identifier field. _2026-08-25 — **Permission-Aware Dashboard Reconciliation — dashboards no longer advertise/leak modules or aggregate data the caller can't access.** Root cause: every card on the main Dashboard (`totalEmployees`, `assetMetrics`, `inventoryMetrics`, and the "Available Modules" registry) was gated only by "did the backend return non-null data" for module-enablement — `leaveMetrics`/`attendanceMetrics` were ALREADY correctly permission-scoped (an established, unmodified precedent this fix extends, not replaces), but `totalEmployees`/`assetMetrics`/`inventoryMetrics` had no permission gate at all, and the module registry cards used the platform-wide build-status catalog (`useListModules`) instead of the organization's actual enablement, with no role/permission check whatsoever. **Backend fix** (`routes/users.ts`, genuine gap, in scope per the task's own Category-A rule): `totalEmployees` now null unless the caller holds `employee.write` (not the broad `employee.read` every role holds — "may view the directory" was never "may see an aggregate headcount"); `assetMetrics`/`inventoryMetrics` now additionally require `asset_management.reports.read`/`office_inventory.reports.read` (the exact permissions each domain's own dashboard page already requires) on top of the existing module-enabled check — no new permission key, no permission-table change, reusing exactly what each domain's own reporting endpoint already gates on. **Frontend fix**: `dashboard.tsx`'s Total Employees tile now follows the same null-omits-the-card contract `leaveMetrics` already established (previously defaulted to a fabricated `0`); the "Available Modules" registry switched from the platform catalog to `useListOrganizationModules` (org-enablement-aware — a module disabled for this org is never shown as "Available") and is now visible only to HR-capable users (informational/administrative overview, no card in it is a functional link). Consolidated the previously-duplicated `isOrgAdmin`/`isHrCapable` role heuristic (independently inlined in `app-shell.tsx` and `use-hr-capable.ts`) into one shared hook, now also used by `dashboard.tsx`; documented in the hook itself exactly where this role-name heuristic is and isn't valid to reach for (asset/inventory/employee dashboard aggregates are real backend permission gates a custom role can hold independently of `hr_manager` — the heuristic must never be used there). Office Inventory's dashboard tab gained the same "Access denied" 403 handling every other per-module dashboard (`assets-dashboard.tsx`, `attendance-dashboard.tsx`, etc.) already had, closing the one dashboard surface that fell back to a generic error instead. Manager Portal's dashboard was inspected and found to already be a correctly-scoped pure orchestration layer (server resolves all authority; no client-side recomputation) — no change needed there, confirming it as the reference pattern this fix extends to the main Dashboard. Backend **2290/2290** (8 new tests: permission-gate coverage for all three metrics, including proof a custom Inventory-only role sees `inventoryMetrics` without `hr_manager`/`org_admin`), frontend typecheck clean, touched suites **72/72**. Live-verified against real WWM personas (no new roles/permissions granted): a plain employee sees Leave/Assets (both intentionally broad-access, unchanged) but never Total Employees or Inventory Items or the module registry; an org_admin (Kwame, no `hr_manager`) sees Total Employees but — proving configuration authority isn't automatically operational authority — never Inventory Items, since no default role grants `office_inventory.reports.read`; a Department Head (Ama) sees neither Total Employees nor Inventory Items despite her departmental authority; the real WWM custom role `wwm_inventory_store_officer` (Nana, holding no `hr_manager`/`org_admin`) correctly sees Inventory Items and nothing else HR-administrative — direct, live proof the composition is permission-driven, not role-name-driven. No schema/migration change (API response shape only). **No Netlify deployment, no production change. WWM's own role/module configuration was not altered.**_

_2026-08-25 — **Fixed: plain employees could open and use HR-only controls on Employees/Branches/Departments/Positions (frontend access-control gap, platform-wide).** Reported symptom: "employees can even add other employees." Root cause investigated and confirmed narrow: the backend was never at fault — `POST /organizations/:id/employees` and every other `employee.write`-gated mutation already correctly returns 403 for a plain `employee` role (live-verified before touching any code). The bug was that the Employees directory and Employee Detail pages (and, found during the same sweep, Branches/Departments/Positions) rendered their mutating controls — Add Employee, Edit, Transfer, Promote, Confirm, Separate, Rehire, Link/Unlink account, upload photo/documents, add/remove skills/qualifications/certifications, personnel-file custody actions, disciplinary records, exit-process fields, Add Branch/Department/Position, Archive/Reactivate, and the inline "move to department/branch" selects — completely unconditionally, with no permission check at all, unlike most other pages in the app (performance-cycles.tsx, asset-workspace.tsx, attendance-register.tsx, etc.) which already gate on an `isHrCapable` role heuristic. A non-privileged viewer could see and click these controls and would only discover they don't work when the request 403'd — a real UX/access-control defect even though no unauthorized write ever actually succeeded. Fixed by extracting the existing per-page heuristic into one shared hook, `useIsHrCapable(organizationId)` (`hooks/use-hr-capable.ts` — org_admin/hr_manager/super_admin, the same role set the backend's own seed data grants `employee.write`/`branch.manage`/`department.manage`/`position.manage` to), and wiring it into all five pages. Department Head assign/revoke controls on the Departments page were deliberately left untouched — they require the separate `department.head.manage` permission, which by design is granted to no standard role (only `super_admin` and any org's own custom role), so the `isHrCapable` heuristic would be actively wrong there; fixing that would need its own, different mechanism, not attempted here. Disclosed limitation carried over from the pre-existing pattern this fix reuses: `isHrCapable` is a role-name heuristic (frontend only has role keys, not the caller's actual permission grants), so a custom per-org role that departs from the standard templates (e.g. an "employee" clone granted `employee.write`) would not be reflected — the backend's own permission check remains the real authority regardless. Frontend typecheck clean; touched suites green (157/157 across branches/employee-detail/employees/employee-self-service/app-shell/profile, including new regression tests proving the controls are hidden for a plain-employee role and still shown for org_admin/hr_manager). Live-verified against real WWM data: Kofi (plain employee) no longer sees Add Employee or any Employee Detail mutating control; Grace (HR) is unaffected. **No backend change, no migration, no Netlify deployment, no production change.**_

_2026-08-24 — **Leave Approval Workflow Reconciliation — Department Head → HR, platform-wide.** Leave's approval authority is reworked from single-stage (direct manager `reportingManagerId` OR org-wide `leave_request.manage`) to a mandatory two-stage flow: Employee submits → the employee's CURRENT Department Head approves/rejects → HR gives final approval/rejection → Approved Leave. Department Head authority is resolved from the existing general `department_heads` primitive (`lib/departmentHeads.ts`, introduced during the Office Inventory epic and confirmed module-agnostic) via a new shared `resolveDepartmentHeadIdentity`/`listDepartmentsHeadedByMembership` pair — re-derived live on every approve/reject call, never cached, never assumed from holding `leave_request.approve` (granted to every employee; it gates "may attempt," not "may act"). One migration (`0055`, purely additive): a new `pending_hr` status value plus 7 new nullable columns on `leave_requests` (`departmentHeadApprovedBy/At`, `departmentHeadRejectedBy/At`, `departmentHeadRejectionReason`, `rejectedBy`, `rejectedAt`) so the Department Head's decision is never overwritten when HR subsequently acts and survives a later Department Head replacement unchanged. A derived (never stored) `workflowStage` — `awaiting_department_head` / `awaiting_hr` / `rejected_by_department_head` / `approved` / `rejected_by_hr` / `cancelled` — is computed server-side and returned on every leave-request response, satisfying "HR sees its exact stage" without a second, duplicated status enum. HR sees every request org-wide from the moment of submission, both stages, but can only act once it reaches "pending_hr" (an early attempt 403s with a stage-specific message); a Department Head sees and can act only on "pending" requests from department(s) they are the CURRENT, actual Head of. Rejection at either stage now requires a non-empty reason (zod `minLength(1)`, both server- and client-enforced); the balance-deducting usage-ledger entry now posts only at final HR approval, not at Department Head approval. `cancelLeaveRequest` extended to also allow withdrawal from "pending_hr". Manager Portal's Leave tiles/pending-actions (which reuse `listPendingApprovals` unchanged, per their own frozen cross-module-authorization invariant) automatically inherit the new Department-Head-scoped authority with no separate code change beyond updating the call sites' argument shape. Frontend: `leave-approvals.tsx` shows a stage badge and the Department Head's decision date, and its reject dialog's reason field is now required; `my-leave.tsx` (ESS) shows the derived stage badge and the applicable rejection reason (Department-Head- or HR-stage, never conflated) — previously invisible even though the backend already stored it. Backend **2282/2282** (23 rewritten + several new Leave-approval tests, plus fixes to Manager Portal/dashboard tests whose mocks used the old signature), workspace typecheck clean, zero schema drift (`drizzle-kit generate` reports "No schema changes" after re-running against the applied migration). Live-verified end-to-end against real WWM data (disposable QA leave type/policy created and archived afterward, per the task's own "disposable development QA scenario" carve-out — WWM's own Leave configuration is otherwise untouched): HR sees a request immediately at submission; HR cannot finally approve before the Department Head; the actual Department Head (Ama, Head of Media & Communications) approves; HR finally approves; a Department Head rejection without a reason 400s, with a reason succeeds and is visible to the employee; an org_admin with no Department Head authority over that department gets 403. **No Netlify deployment, no production change. WWM's own role/module configuration was not altered.**_

Full record: `docs/WWM_ORGANIZATION_SETUP.md` §12–§15, cleanup manifest in `docs/WWM_PRESENTATION_DEMO_DATA.md`. **No Netlify deployment, no production change.**_

**Branding — tenant-scoped, not hardcoded.** New `theme` field on the existing `branding` config namespace: 9 optional HSL-triple tokens mapped directly onto `index.css`'s existing CSS custom properties (`--sidebar`, `--primary`, `--ring`, ...) — not a general theming engine, a fixed small set. `TenantTheme` (new, mounted once in `App.tsx`) applies them as inline style overrides on `document.documentElement`, always clearing all nine first so one tenant's colours can never bleed into another's render. Because the shell already consumed these variables (`bg-sidebar`, `bg-primary`, `focus-visible:ring-ring`) before this workstream touched anything, setting WWM's navy/gold values reskinned the entire authenticated app and login page with no further per-page edits — verified with live screenshots (Playwright, browser already cached locally) of the login page and an HR dashboard, both correctly navy/white/gold, and of Acme staying on the untouched default theme.

**Login/shell refinement.** Login's left panel changed from a gradient wash to a solid `primary` panel with a thin `accent` wave divider (accent used sparingly, per the approved direction); mobile logo block now also shows the resolved tenant logo. The authenticated shell's previously-separate hardcoded "Enterprise HRMS" header and the tenant-aware org pill were consolidated into one `OrgBrandHeader`/`OrgBrandSwitcher` (logo + name + system display name, sourced from `MembershipSummary`, which gained `systemDisplayName` resolved per the caller's *active* org). The header's decorative, non-functional search box (`readOnly`, did nothing when typed into) was removed rather than kept as a control that only looks functional — matching the request's own explicit instruction against exactly that pattern. The sidebar's redundant "Notifications" entry was removed (the header's own working bell already covers it).

**Navigation regrouped, not rebuilt.** The sidebar's ~50-item flat list (accumulated over many workstreams, one per shipped module/page) was reorganized into 11 labelled, collapsible sections via a new `NavGroupList` component — every underlying href and every `isHrCapable`/`isOrgAdmin` visibility condition is byte-for-byte unchanged, this is a rendering change only. A group with zero visible items renders no header. Verified live: a plain employee (Kofi) sees only Self-Service/Leave Management groups; HR (Grace) sees all groups her role is entitled to.

**Dashboard — real data only.** `GET /dashboard/summary` gained three more null-when-disabled metric groups (`attendanceMetrics`, `assetMetrics`, `inventoryMetrics`), following the exact `leaveMetrics` precedent exactly — `attendanceMetrics` reuses the existing W70 Attendance Dashboard aggregation and its own visibility scope, the other two are lightweight counts matching the pre-existing `totalEmployees` style. None are fabricated; all are null until their module is enabled. **Bug found and fixed:** switching organizations never invalidated `dashboard/summary`'s query (its key carries no parameters — the route resolves everything from the server session) — a caller who switched orgs kept seeing the *previous* organization's dashboard numbers. Fixed with one additional `invalidateQueries` call, covered by a new regression test, verified live via network trace (before: stale org-1 numbers after switching to WWM; after: WWM's real `0 employees / 1 active module / 0 inventory items`).

**Presentation demo data — approved this workstream, unlike Workstream 1.** Six clearly-recognizable presentation identities (`@wwm.test` emails) created entirely through the real application flows: `POST /organizations/:id/invitations` → `POST /invitations/:token/accept` for account creation (never a raw password-hash write — this session's own safety controls correctly refused that for the one pre-existing account too, so `POST /auth/forgot-password` → read-only token lookup → `POST /auth/reset-password/:token` was used instead, the same flow a real user's "forgot password" click would trigger), then the ordinary employee/department/position/role/module HTTP APIs for everything else. Full lifecycle demonstrated live: Office Inventory store → items → receiving → an employee request approved by the Department Head and issued by a dedicated Store Officer role (a fourth custom WWM role, `wwm_department_head`, had to be added — the delegation-creation route requires the caller to be *both* permission-holding and the department's actual current Head, which no existing role combination satisfied) → a second request deliberately left pending to show the live approval queue. Two assets assigned, two real attendance clock-ins. `attendance`, `asset_management`, `employee_self_service` modules enabled for WWM; `leave` remains untouched (hidden platform-wide, unrelated to WWM). Full manifest and removal instructions in `docs/WWM_PRESENTATION_DEMO_DATA.md`.

**Findings disclosed, not silently resolved:** no biometric/device attendance architecture exists anywhere in the codebase (self-service software clock-in is the only capture mechanism, and is fully sufficient — not a gap this workstream needed to fill); the PIF/Leave Form document-generation finding from Workstream 1 (no such generator exists in this repository) stands unchanged, re-confirmed rather than re-investigated.

**Tests:** `tenant-theme.test.tsx` (new, 4 cases — theme application/isolation/clearing), `app-shell.test.tsx` (+9 cases — logo/systemDisplayName rendering, nav grouping/collapse, Notifications/search removal, the org-switch dashboard-invalidation regression), `dashboard.test.tsx` (+2 cases — new metric cards present/absent), `login.test.tsx` fixture types extended. Backend: two existing tenant-context tests updated for the new `theme: null` field. No demo-data creation has a dedicated automated test (it is operational configuration created via live HTTP calls, not application code) — its correctness was verified live instead, per §21's "focused tests while implementing, full regression once stable" instruction.

**Commit / Push:** see this entry's commit for the exact file list. **Production: UNTOUCHED. Netlify: NOT DEPLOYED.**

What the investigation did find already fully built: the hostname-based tenant-resolution and login-branding infrastructure (`organization_domains`, `resolveTenantHost`, `GET /tenant-context`, and — already, before this workstream touched it — `login.tsx` itself already calling `useGetTenantContext()` and rendering a resolved organization's name/logo with an "Enterprise HRMS" fallback). `organizations.name`/`organizations.logoUrl` already existed as columns. _Previously last updated: 2026-08-24 — **Office Inventory Management, Workstream 12 — Completion Report: OFFICE INVENTORY COMPLETE.** Formal, documentation-only closure of the entire Office Inventory implementation, mirroring Payroll's own Frozen Workstream 10 closure precedent — **zero application-code changes, zero migrations, zero schema changes, zero permission changes, Office Inventory not enabled for WWM or any organization, production untouched.** **Workstream 11 PASS (commit `e63090c`) is used as the standing verification authority and is not re-derived here** — this report performed only the lightweight reconciliation needed to confirm that verified state has not since drifted: re-confirmed local `main == origin/main` at `e63090c`; `git status` unchanged from session start (only the same pre-existing, unrelated untracked items); migration ledger re-read directly, still ends at `0054`; `drizzle-kit generate` reports zero schema drift. No test suite, build, or live QA was re-run, since none of that state could have been affected by a documentation-only edit.

**Final delivered scope:** module/configuration foundation; organization-defined item categories, consumable/returnable classification, permanent item codes; flat stores with permanent codes; the append-only `office_inventory_stock_movements` ledger as sole stock authority; multi-item atomic receiving; employee and department requests; repeat-request accountability warnings (informational, non-blocking, real W4-W7 custody/issue/return data, no scoring); Department Head approval including permanently-valid self-approval; approval delegation with historically-traceable authority snapshots; partial approval; issue/fulfilment (request-based and direct) with mandatory direct-issue reason and config gate; non-gating receipt confirmation; live-derived employee and department custody with expected-return-date/overdue derivation; returns (full/partial, over-return rejected); handovers (all four holder-type directions); atomic store transfers; damage/missing incident reporting (zero ledger effect) with separate mark-missing/recovery/write-off actions; store-only adjustments; full stocktaking (draft→counting→finalized, DB-clock snapshot, mandatory variance resolution, finalization immutability); ESS "My Inventory" (own requests/custody/history/return/handover/damage-missing, `resolveOwnEmployeeId`-scoped); the Department Head accountability UX (repeat-request/custody context, delegate display); a live-derived dashboard (13 tiles, no persisted aggregate); the 13 frozen reports with hardened, formula-injection-safe CSV export; the explicit, permission-gated, one-directional Assets Handoff (one unit per action, no dual custody); full mutation audit coverage; tenant isolation; historical-identity integrity (`employees.id`/`departments.id`, never staff number); and concurrency/idempotency protection on every balance-affecting action.

**Core accountability model, stated for the record:** stock authority is exclusively `office_inventory_stock_movements` — current stock and custody are always live-derived, never a cached competing value; every historical movement is retained permanently. Employee identity is `employees.id`; department identity is `departments.id`; a staff number is display-only, never identity. A department change never silently relocates personal custody. Employee separation never silently returns stock (warn-only, via Outstanding Returns — no coupling to `separateEmployee()`). Staff-number release-and-reuse never transfers historical accountability to the new holder of that number. Together these let the system answer, at any time: what came in, where it went, who currently holds it, which department holds it, what was returned, what was handed over, what is overdue, what went missing, what was damaged, what was recovered, what was written off, what was adjusted, what was converted into an Asset, and who performed or approved each action.

**Request/approval accountability:** a repeat request within the organization-configurable review window surfaces the requesting employee's and department's prior request history plus real current custody and recent issue/return activity to the Department Head — informational and non-blocking only, never a fraud/suspicion score, never an automatic rejection; the Head may always still approve. Department Head approval (including self-approval, frozen permanently) and authorized, historically-snapshotted delegation are the only two approval-authority paths — never a generic permission grant alone, never a `reportingManagerId` fallback.

**Inventory/Procurement boundary:** Office Inventory manages stock already received into or held by the organization. It implements no requisition workflow, no RFQ, no purchase order, no supplier-ordering workflow, no accounts payable, no payment processing. Receiving `source`/`deliveryReference` fields are descriptive free text only, structurally incapable of driving a procurement workflow.

**Inventory/Assets boundary:** Office Inventory owns quantity/store/custody accountability; Assets owns individually-tracked durable property. The one bridge between them is the Assets Handoff — explicit, manual, `office_inventory.asset_handoff`-gated, Inventory→Asset only, exactly one unit per action, fully traceable in both directions via `sourceReferenceType='asset'`, with no dual custody possible. No reverse Asset→Inventory workflow exists in V1.

**Security/access model, final count:** 23 relevant permission keys — 22 `office_inventory.*` plus the one general `department.head.manage` (the earlier "22 keys total" figure in the frozen plan's own §38 prose is a documentation undercount by one; the actual registered, live-queried, W11-confirmed total is 23). None of the 22 `office_inventory.*` keys nor `department.head.manage` are granted by default to `employee`, `hr_manager`, or `org_admin` — `super_admin` alone retains the platform's existing blanket-grant behavior. This is deliberate: an organization assigns operational Inventory access explicitly, exactly as Payroll already established; WWM HR can later be granted the full operational set through the ordinary role/permission mechanism without any Inventory authority ever being hard-coded to the `hr_manager` role. Employees reach ESS capabilities only through whichever `.own`-suffixed or no-permission-required "own" routes the frozen design actually grants (never a client-supplied identity); Department Heads receive approval authority only through the live, relationship-derived `department_heads`/delegation resolution — never a role label, never `reportingManagerId`.

**W11 verification authority (cited, not rerun):** PASS — master scenario 57/57; backend 123/123 files, 2249/2249 tests; frontend 64/64 files, 724/724 tests; full typecheck clean; all 3 production builds clean; zero schema drift; RLS 121/121 tables at 100%, zero policies; tenant isolation PASS; historical integrity PASS; staff-number reuse PASS; department-change integrity PASS; separation accountability PASS; Assets Handoff cross-module atomicity challenge (concurrent last-unit race, forced-failure atomicity, idempotent replay) PASS; Category A defects: none.

**Schema/migration footprint (from repository reality, not invented):** migration ledger ends at `0054`, unchanged by this workstream. Office Inventory's own tables: `office_inventory_items`, `office_inventory_stores`, `office_inventory_stock_movements`, `office_inventory_requests`, `office_inventory_request_lines`, `office_inventory_approval_delegations`, `office_inventory_incidents`, `office_inventory_stocktakes`, `office_inventory_stocktake_lines` — plus the general, non-Inventory-owned `department_heads` table (an organizational-authority primitive, §5.1, reusable by any future module). No `office_inventory_evidence`/attachment table was ever actually built in the delivered workstream sequence (§41 of the frozen plan named it as in-scope; it was not exercised by any shipped workstream and carries no rows) — recorded here for accuracy rather than silently implied as delivered.
